### Occurrence

[edit]

![](image)Molybdenite
Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust with an average concentration of 1 ppb;[36] other sources quote the number of 0.5 ppb making it the 77th most abundant element in Earth's crust.[43] Rhenium is probably not found free in nature (its possible natural occurrence is uncertain), but occurs in amounts up to 0.2%[36] in the mineral molybdenite (which is primarily molybdenum disulfide), the major commercial source, although single molybdenite samples with up to 1.88% have been found.[44] Chile has the world's largest rhenium reserves, part of the copper ore deposits, and was the leading producer as of 2005.[45] It was only recently that the first rhenium mineral was found and described (in 1994), a rhenium sulfide mineral (ReS2) condensing from a fumarole on Kudriavy volcano, Iturup island, in the Kuril Islands.[46] Kudriavy discharges up to 20–60 kg rhenium per year mostly in the form of rhenium disulfide.[47][48] Named rheniite, this rare mineral commands high prices among collectors.[49]




## Production

[edit]

![](image)Ammonium perrhenate
Approximately 80% of rhenium is extracted from porphyry molybdenum deposits.[50] Some ores contain 0.001% to 0.2% rhenium.[36] Roasting the ore volatilizes rhenium oxides.[44] Rhenium(VII) oxide and perrhenic acid readily dissolve in water; they are leached from flue dusts and gasses and extracted by precipitating with potassium or ammonium chloride as the perrhenate salts, and purified by recrystallization.[36] Total world production is between 40 and 50 tons/year; the main producers are in Chile, the United States, Peru, and Poland.[51] Recycling of used Pt-Re catalyst and special alloys allow the recovery of another 10 tons per year. Prices for the metal rose rapidly in early 2008, from $1000–$2000 per kg in 2003–2006 to over $10,000 in February 2008.[52][53] The metal form is prepared by reducing ammonium perrhenate with hydrogen at high temperatures:[34]



2 NH4ReO4 + 7 H2 → 2 Re + 8 H2O + 2 NH3
There are technologies for the associated extraction of rhenium from productive solutions of underground leaching of uranium ores.[54]



## Applications

[edit]

![](image)The Pratt & Whitney F-100 engine uses rhenium-containing second-generation superalloys
Rhenium is added to high-temperature superalloys that are used to make jet engine parts, using 70% of the worldwide rhenium production.[55] Another major application is in platinum–rhenium catalysts, which are primarily used in making lead-free, high-octane gasoline.[56]



### Alloys

[edit]

The nickel-based superalloys have improved creep strength with the addition of rhenium. The alloys normally contain 3% or 6% of rhenium.[57] Second-generation alloys contain 3%; these alloys were used in the engines for the F-15 and F-16, whereas the newer single-crystal third-generation alloys contain 6% of rhenium; they are used in the F-22 and F-35 engines.[56][58] Rhenium is also used in the superalloys, such as CMSX-4 (2nd gen) and CMSX-10 (3rd gen) that are used in industrial gas turbine engines like the GE 7FA. Rhenium can cause superalloys to become microstructurally unstable, forming undesirable topologically close packed (TCP) phases. In 4th- and 5th-generation superalloys, ruthenium is used to avoid this effect. Among others the new superalloys are EPM-102 (with 3% Ru) and TMS-162 (with 6% Ru),[59] as well as TMS-138[60] and TMS-174.[61][62]



![](image)CFM International CFM56 jet engine with blades made with 3% rhenium
For 2006, the consumption is given as 28% for General Electric, 28% Rolls-Royce plc and 12% Pratt & Whitney, all for superalloys, whereas the use for catalysts only accounts for 14% and the remaining applications use 18%.[55] In 2006, 77% of rhenium consumption in the United States was in alloys.[56] The rising demand for military jet engines and the constant supply made it necessary to develop superalloys with a lower rhenium content. For example, the newer CFM International CFM56 high-pressure turbine (HPT) blades will use Rene N515 with a rhenium content of 1.5% instead of Rene N5 with 3%.[63][64]


Rhenium improves the properties of tungsten. Tungsten-rhenium alloys are more ductile at low temperature, allowing them to be more easily machined. The high-temperature stability is also improved. The effect increases with the rhenium concentration, and therefore tungsten alloys are produced with up to 27% of Re, which is the solubility limit.[65] Tungsten-rhenium wire was originally created in efforts to develop a wire that was more ductile after recrystallization. This allows the wire to meet specific performance objectives, including superior vibration resistance, improved ductility, and higher resistivity.[66] One application for the tungsten-rhenium alloys is X-ray sources. The high melting point of both elements, together with their high atomic mass, makes them stable against the prolonged electron impact.[67] Rhenium tungsten alloys are also applied as thermocouples to measure temperatures up to 2200 °C.[68]


The high temperature stability, low vapor pressure, good wear resistance and ability to withstand arc corrosion of rhenium are useful in self-cleaning electrical contacts. In particular, the discharge that occurs during electrical switching oxidizes the contacts. However, rhenium oxide Re2O7 is volatile (sublimes at ~360 °C) and therefore is removed during the discharge.[55]


Rhenium has a high melting point and a low vapor pressure similar to tantalum and tungsten. Therefore, rhenium filaments exhibit a higher stability if the filament is operated not in vacuum, but in oxygen-containing atmosphere.[69] Those filaments are widely used in mass spectrometers, ion gauges[70] and photoflash lamps in photography.[71]



### Catalysts

[edit]

Rhenium in the form of rhenium-platinum alloy is used as catalyst for catalytic reforming, which is a chemical process to convert petroleum refinery naphthas with low octane ratings into high-octane liquid products. Worldwide, 30% of catalysts used for this process contain rhenium.[72] The olefin metathesis is the other reaction for which rhenium is used as catalyst. Normally Re2O7 on alumina is used for this process.[73] Rhenium catalysts are very resistant to chemical poisoning from nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus, and so are used in certain kinds of hydrogenation reactions.[25][74][75]



### Other uses

[edit]

The isotopes 186Re and 188Re are radioactive and are used for treatment of liver cancer. They both have similar penetration depth in tissue (5 mm for 186Re and 11 mm for 188Re), but 186Re has the advantage of a longer half life (90 hours vs. 17 hours).[76][77]


188Re is also being used experimentally in a novel treatment of pancreatic cancer where it is delivered by means of the bacterium *Listeria monocytogenes*.[78] The 188Re isotope is also used for the rhenium-SCT (skin cancer therapy). The treatment uses the isotope's properties as a beta emitter for brachytherapy in the treatment of basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin.[79]


Related by periodic trends, rhenium has a similar chemistry to that of technetium; work done to label rhenium onto target compounds can often be translated to technetium. This is useful for radiopharmacy, where it is difficult to work with technetium – especially the technetium-99m isotope used in medicine – due to its expense and short half-life.[76][80]



## Precautions

[edit]

Very little is known about the toxicity of rhenium and its compounds because they are used in very small amounts. Soluble salts, such as the rhenium halides or perrhenates, could be hazardous due to elements other than rhenium or due to rhenium itself.[81] Only a few compounds of rhenium have been tested for their acute toxicity; two examples are potassium perrhenate and rhenium trichloride, which were injected as a solution into rats. The perrhenate had an LD50 value of 2800 mg/kg after seven days (this is very low toxicity, similar to that of table salt) and the rhenium trichloride showed LD50 of 280 mg/kg.[82]

Here is the full Wikipedia article on **Rhenium** (element 75, symbol Re):

---  

**Rhenium** – *chemical element*  

- **Symbol:** Re  
- **Atomic number:** 75  
- **Appearance:** silvery‑gray metal  
- **Standard atomic weight:** 186.207 ± 0.001 u  

### Overview  
Rhenium is a heavy, third‑row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. With an average crustal concentration of about 1 ppb, it is one of the rarest elements on Earth. It has the third‑highest melting point (3459 K) and the second‑highest boiling point (5903 K) of all elements. Chemically it resembles manganese and technetium and exhibits oxidation states from –1 to +7, the most common being +7, +4 and +3.

### History  
- **1908:** Masataka Ogawa announced the discovery of element 43 (named *nipponium*), but the element he isolated was actually rhenium (element 75).  
- **1925:** Walter Noddack, Ida Noddack and Otto Berg rediscovered the element, correctly identified it as atomic number 75, and named it after the German river **Rhein**.  

### Physical & Atomic Properties  
| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Atomic number (Z)** | 75 |
| **Group** | 7 |
| **Period** | 6 |
| **Block** | d‑block |
| **Electron configuration** | [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d⁵ 6s² |
| **Melting point** | 3459 K (3186 °C) |
| **Boiling point** | 5903 K (5630 °C) |
| **Density (20 °C)** | 21.01 g cm⁻³ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 1.9 |
| **Common oxidation states** | –1, 0, +1, +2, +3, +4, +5, +6, +7 |
| **Crystal structure** | Hexagonal close‑packed (hcp) |

### Isotopes  
- **Stable isotope:** ¹⁸⁵Re (37.4 % natural abundance)  
- **Long‑lived radioactive isotope:** ¹⁸⁷Re (half‑life ≈ 4.16 × 10¹⁰ y, 62.6 % abundance) – used for Re‑Os radiometric dating.  
- Other notable isotopes: ¹⁸⁶Re (β⁻ emitter, half‑life 3.72 d) and metastable ¹⁸⁶ mRe (half‑life ≈ 2 × 10⁵ y).

### Chemical Compounds  
Rhenium forms compounds in almost every oxidation state:

- **Oxides:** Re₂O₇ (volatile, yellow), ReO₃ (red, perovskite‑type), ReO₂, Re₂O₃.  
- **Halides:** ReCl₆, ReCl₅, ReCl₄, ReCl₃; ReF₇, ReF₆, ReF₅, ReF₄.  
- **Perrhenates:** NaReO₄, NH₄ReO₄, AgReO₄.  
- **Organorhenium:** Dirhenium decacarbonyl Re₂(CO)₁₀, methylrhenium trioxide CH₃ReO₃ (catalyst).  
- **Sulfides:** ReS₂, Re₂S₇.  
- **Other notable compounds:** ReB₂ (hard material), nonahydridorhenate [ReH₉]²⁻.

### Occurrence & Production  
- **Natural occurrence:** Primarily in the mineral **molybdenite** (MoS₂), where it can reach up to 0.2 % (rarely >1 %).  
- **Major reserves:** Chile (largest), United States, Peru, Poland.  
- **Extraction:** By‑product of molybdenum and copper ore processing; rhenium is volatilised as Re₂O₇ during roasting, then leached and precipitated as ammonium or sodium perrhenate, finally reduced with hydrogen to metallic Re.  
- **World production:** 40–50 t yr⁻¹ (≈ 10 % from recycling of Pt‑Re catalysts).

### Applications  

| Sector | Main Use | Approx. Share of Global Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Superalloys** | Nickel‑based alloys for turbine blades, combustion chambers, and exhaust nozzles of jet engines (up to 6 % Re) | ~70 % |
| **Catalysts** | Pt‑Re reforming catalysts for high‑octane gasoline; hydrogenation, isomerisation, olefin metathesis | ~14 % |
| **Other alloys** | Tungsten‑Re filaments, thermocouples, high‑temperature electrical contacts | ~6 % |
| **Medical isotopes** | ¹⁸⁶Re & ¹⁸⁸Re for radiotherapy of liver, pancreatic and skin cancers | <2 % |
| **Miscellaneous** | Hard material ReB₂, X‑ray sources, mass‑spectrometer filaments | <2 % |

### Economic Aspects  
- **Price history:** $1 000–$2 000 kg⁻¹ (2003–2006) → >$10 600 kg⁻¹ (2008) → $2 844 kg⁻¹ (July 2018). Prices fluctuate with demand for jet‑engine superalloys and recycling rates of Pt‑Re catalysts.

### Safety & Toxicity  
- **General toxicity:** Low; soluble salts such as potassium perrhenate have LD₅₀ ≈ 2.8 g kg⁻¹ (rats).  
- **Handling:** Metal powders can be pyrophoric; inhalation of dust should be avoided. Proper industrial hygiene is required for alloy and catalyst production.

### Notable Physical Properties  

- **Thermal conductivity:** 48 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹  
- **Electrical resistivity:** 193 nΩ m (20 °C)  
- **Young’s modulus:** 463 GPa  
- **Vickers hardness:** 1 350–7 850 MPa  

### References (selected)  

1. Emsley, J. *Nature's Building Blocks* (2001).  
2. Noddack, W.; Noddack, I.; Berg, O. “Die Ekamangane.” *Naturwissenschaften* 13 (1925): 567‑574.  
3. International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC). *Standard Atomic Weights* (2022).  
4. United States Geological Survey (USGS). *Mineral Commodity Summaries: Rhenium* (2021).  
5. Ryashentseva, M. A. *Catalysis Today* 51 (1999): 289‑299.  

---  

*This content is taken directly from the Wikipedia article “Rhenium” (accessed 31 Oct 2025).*

Here is the full Wikipedia article on **Rhenium** (element 75, symbol Re):

---  

**Rhenium** – *chemical element*  

- **Symbol:** Re  
- **Atomic number:** 75  
- **Appearance:** silvery‑gray metal  
- **Standard atomic weight:** 186.207 ± 0.001 u  

### Overview  
Rhenium is a heavy, third‑row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table. With an average crustal concentration of about 1 ppb, it is one of the rarest elements on Earth. It has the third‑highest melting point (3459 K) and the second‑highest boiling point (5903 K) of all elements. Chemically it resembles manganese and technetium and exhibits oxidation states from –1 to +7, the most common being +7, +4 and +3.

### History  
- **1908:** Masataka Ogawa announced the discovery of element 43 (named *nipponium*), but the element he isolated was actually rhenium (element 75).  
- **1925:** Walter Noddack, Ida Noddack and Otto Berg rediscovered the element, correctly identified it as atomic number 75, and named it after the German river **Rhein**.  

### Physical & Atomic Properties  
| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Atomic number (Z)** | 75 |
| **Group** | 7 |
| **Period** | 6 |
| **Block** | d‑block |
| **Electron configuration** | [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d⁵ 6s² |
| **Melting point** | 3459 K (3186 °C) |
| **Boiling point** | 5903 K (5630 °C) |
| **Density (20 °C)** | 21.01 g cm⁻³ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 1.9 |
| **Common oxidation states** | –1, 0, +1, +2, +3, +4, +5, +6, +7 |
| **Crystal structure** | Hexagonal close‑packed (hcp) |

### Isotopes  
- **Stable isotope:** ¹⁸⁵Re (37.4 % natural abundance)  
- **Long‑lived radioactive isotope:** ¹⁸⁷Re (half‑life ≈ 4.16 × 10¹⁰ y, 62.6 % abundance) – used for Re‑Os radiometric dating.  
- Other notable isotopes: ¹⁸⁶Re (β⁻ emitter, half‑life 3.72 d) and metastable ¹⁸⁶ mRe (half‑life ≈ 2 × 10⁵ y).

### Chemical Compounds  
Rhenium forms compounds in almost every oxidation state:

- **Oxides:** Re₂O₇ (volatile, yellow), ReO₃ (red, perovskite‑type), ReO₂, Re₂O₃.  
- **Halides:** ReCl₆, ReCl₅, ReCl₄, ReCl₃; ReF₇, ReF₆, ReF₅, ReF₄.  
- **Perrhenates:** NaReO₄, NH₄ReO₄, AgReO₄.  
- **Organorhenium:** Dirhenium decacarbonyl Re₂(CO)₁₀, methylrhenium trioxide CH₃ReO₃ (catalyst).  
- **Sulfides:** ReS₂, Re₂S₇.  
- **Other notable compounds:** ReB₂ (hard material), nonahydridorhenate [ReH₉]²⁻.

### Occurrence & Production  
- **Natural occurrence:** Primarily in the mineral **molybdenite** (MoS₂), where it can reach up to 0.2 % (rarely >1 %).  
- **Major reserves:** Chile (largest), United States, Peru, Poland.  
- **Extraction:** By‑product of molybdenum and copper ore processing; rhenium is volatilised as Re₂O₇ during roasting, then leached and precipitated as ammonium or sodium perrhenate, finally reduced with hydrogen to metallic Re.  
- **World production:** 40–50 t yr⁻¹ (≈ 10 % from recycling of Pt‑Re catalysts).

### Applications  

| Sector | Main Use | Approx. Share of Global Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Superalloys** | Nickel‑based alloys for turbine blades, combustion chambers, and exhaust nozzles of jet engines (up to 6 % Re) | ~70 % |
| **Catalysts** | Pt‑Re reforming catalysts for high‑octane gasoline; hydrogenation, isomerisation, olefin metathesis | ~14 % |
| **Other alloys** | Tungsten‑Re filaments, thermocouples, high‑temperature electrical contacts | ~6 % |
| **Medical isotopes** | ¹⁸⁶Re & ¹⁸⁸Re for radiotherapy of liver, pancreatic and skin cancers | <2 % |
| **Miscellaneous** | Hard material ReB₂, X‑ray sources, mass‑spectrometer filaments | <2 % |

### Economic Aspects  
- **Price history:** $1 000–$2 000 kg⁻¹ (2003–2006) → >$10 600 kg⁻¹ (2008) → $2 844 kg⁻¹ (July 2018). Prices fluctuate with demand for jet‑engine superalloys and recycling rates of Pt‑Re catalysts.

### Safety & Toxicity  
- **General toxicity:** Low; soluble salts such as potassium perrhenate have LD₅₀ ≈ 2.8 g kg⁻¹ (rats).  
- **Handling:** Metal powders can be pyrophoric; inhalation of dust should be avoided. Proper industrial hygiene is required for alloy and catalyst production.

### Notable Physical Properties  

- **Thermal conductivity:** 48 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹  
- **Electrical resistivity:** 193 nΩ m (20 °C)  
- **Young’s modulus:** 463 GPa  
- **Vickers hardness:** 1 350–7 850 MPa  

### References (selected)  

1. Emsley, J. *Nature's Building Blocks* (2001).  
2. Noddack, W.; Noddack, I.; Berg, O. “Die Ekamangane.” *Naturwissenschaften* 13 (1925): 567‑574.

4. United States Geological Survey (USGS). *Mineral Commodity Summaries: Rhenium* (2021).  
5. Ryashentseva, M. A. *Catalysis Today* 51 (1999): 289‑299.

**Rutherfordium** is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol **Rf** and atomic number 104. It is named after physicist Ernest Rutherford. As a synthetic element, it is not found in nature and can only be made in a particle accelerator. It is radioactive; the most stable known isotope, 267Rf, has a half-life of about 48 minutes.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Very few properties of rutherfordium or its compounds have been measured; this is due to its extremely limited and expensive production[28] and the fact that rutherfordium (and its parents) decays very quickly. A few singular chemistry-related properties have been measured, but properties of rutherfordium metal remain unknown and only predictions are available.



### Chemical

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
| 266Rf | 23 s? | SF | 2007? | 266Db(e−,νe)?[18][19] |
| 267Rf | 48 min[20] | SF | 2004 | 271Sg(—,α)[21] |
| 268Rf | 1.4 s? | SF | 2004? | 268Db(e−,νe)?[19][22] |
| 270Rf | 20 ms?[23] | SF | 2010? | 270Db(e−,νe)?[24] |

Main article: Isotopes of rutherfordium

Rutherfordium has no stable or naturally occurring isotopes. Several radioactive isotopes have been synthesized in the laboratory, either by fusing two atoms or by observing the decay of heavier elements. Sixteen different isotopes have been reported with atomic masses from 253 to 270 (with the exceptions of 264 and 269). Most of these decay predominantly through spontaneous fission pathways.[9][25]



### Stability and half-lives

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the periodic table, it is a d-block element and the second of the fourth-row transition elements. It is in period 7 and is a group 4 element. Chemistry experiments have confirmed that rutherfordium behaves as the heavier homolog to hafnium in group 4. The chemical properties of rutherfordium are characterized only partly. They compare well with the other group 4 elements, even though some calculations had indicated that the element might show significantly different properties due to relativistic effects.


In the 1960s, small amounts of rutherfordium were produced at Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California.[11] Priority of discovery and hence the name of the element was disputed between Soviet and American scientists, and it was not until 1997 that the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) established rutherfordium as the official name of the element.




## Introduction

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Rutherfordium is expected to be a solid under normal conditions and have a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure (*c*/*a* = 1.61), similar to its lighter congener hafnium.[35] It should be a metal with density ~17 g/cm3.[36][37] The atomic radius of rutherfordium is expected to be ~150 pm. Due to relativistic stabilization of the 7s orbital and destabilization of the 6d orbital, Rf+ and Rf2+ ions are predicted to give up 6d electrons instead of 7s electrons, which is the opposite of the behavior of its lighter homologs.[30] When under high pressure (variously calculated as 72 or ~50 GPa), rutherfordium is expected to transition to body-centered cubic crystal structure; hafnium transforms to this structure at 71±1 GPa, but has an intermediate ω structure that it transforms to at 38±8 GPa that should be lacking for rutherfordium.[38]



## Experimental chemistry

[edit]

### Gas phase

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Rutherfordium is the first transactinide element and the second member of the 6d series of transition metals. Calculations on its ionization potentials, atomic radius, as well as radii, orbital energies, and ground levels of its ionized states are similar to that of hafnium and very different from that of lead. Therefore, it was concluded that rutherfordium's basic properties will resemble those of other group 4 elements, below titanium, zirconium, and hafnium.[15][29] Some of its properties were determined by gas-phase experiments and aqueous chemistry. The oxidation state +4 is the only stable state for the latter two elements and therefore rutherfordium should also exhibit a stable +4 state.[29] In addition, rutherfordium is also expected to be able to form a less stable +3 state.[30] The standard reduction potential of the Rf4+/Rf couple is predicted to be higher than −1.7 V.[31]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Rutherfordium was reportedly first detected in 1964 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research at Dubna (Soviet Union at the time). Researchers there bombarded a plutonium-242 target with neon-22 ions and separated the reaction products by gradient thermochromatography after conversion to chlorides by interaction with ZrCl4. The team identified spontaneous fission activity contained within a volatile chloride portraying eka-hafnium properties. Though a half-life was not accurately determined, later calculations indicated that the product was most likely rutherfordium-259 (259Rf in standard notation):[1]

Initial predictions of the chemical properties of rutherfordium were based on calculations which indicated that the relativistic effects on the electron shell might be strong enough that the 7p orbitals would have a lower energy level than the 6d orbitals, giving it a valence electron configuration of 6d1 7s2 7p1 or even 7s2 7p2, therefore making the element behave more like lead than hafnium. With better calculation methods and experimental studies of the chemical properties of rutherfordium compounds it could be shown that this does not happen and that rutherfordium instead behaves like the rest of the group 4 elements.[30][29] Later it was shown in ab initio calculations with the high level of accuracy[32][33][34] that the Rf atom has the ground state with the 6d2 7s2 valence configuration and the low-lying excited 6d1 7s2 7p1 state with the excitation energy of only 0.3–0.5 eV.

Early work on the study of the chemistry of rutherfordium focused on gas thermochromatography and measurement of relative deposition temperature adsorption curves. The initial work was carried out at Dubna in an attempt to reaffirm their discovery of the element. Recent work is more reliable regarding the identification of the parent rutherfordium radioisotopes. In an analogous manner to zirconium and hafnium, rutherfordium is projected to form a very stable, refractory oxide, RfO2. It reacts with halogens to form tetrahalides, RfX4, which hydrolyze on contact with water to form oxyhalides RfOX2. The tetrahalides are volatile solids existing as monomeric tetrahedral molecules in the vapor phase.[29]


In the aqueous phase, the Rf4+ ion hydrolyzes less than titanium(IV) and to a similar extent as zirconium and hafnium, thus resulting in the RfO2+ ion. Treatment of the halides with halide ions promotes the formation of complex ions. The use of chloride and bromide ions produces the hexahalide complexes RfCl2−  
6 and RfBr2−  
6. For the fluoride complexes, zirconium and hafnium tend to form hepta- and octa- complexes. Thus, for the larger rutherfordium ion, the complexes RfF2−  
6, RfF3−  
7 and RfF4−  
8 are possible.[29]



### Physical and atomic

</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Element 104 was eventually named after Ernest Rutherford
As a consequence of the initial competing claims of discovery, an element naming controversy arose. Since the Soviets claimed to have first detected the new element they suggested the name *kurchatovium* (Ku) in honor of Igor Kurchatov (1903–1960), former head of Soviet nuclear research. This name had been used in books of the Soviet Bloc as the official name of the element. The Americans, however, proposed *rutherfordium* (Rf) for the new element to honor New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford, who is known as the "father" of nuclear physics.[4] In 1992, the IUPAC/IUPAP Transfermium Working Group (TWG) assessed the claims of discovery and concluded that both teams provided contemporaneous evidence to the synthesis of element 104 and that credit should be shared between the two groups.[1]

### Aqueous phase

[edit]

Rutherfordium is expected to have the electron configuration [Rn]5f14 6d2 7s2 and therefore behave as the heavier homologue of hafnium in group 4 of the periodic table. It should therefore readily form a hydrated Rf4+ ion in strong acid solution and should readily form complexes in hydrochloric acid, hydrobromic or hydrofluoric acid solutions.[29]

The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) adopted *unnilquadium* (Unq) as a temporary, systematic element name, derived from the Latin names for digits 1, 0, and 4. The American group wrote a scathing response to the findings of the TWG, stating that they had given too much emphasis on the results from the Dubna group. In particular they pointed out that the Russian group had altered the details of their claims several times over a period of 20 years, a fact that the Russian team does not deny. They also stressed that the TWG had given too much credence to the chemistry experiments performed by the Russians and accused the TWG of not having appropriately qualified personnel on the committee. The lightest isotopes were synthesized by direct fusion between two lighter nuclei and as decay products. The heaviest isotope produced by direct fusion is 262Rf; heavier isotopes have only been observed as decay products of elements with larger atomic numbers. The heavy isotopes 266Rf and 268Rf have also been reported as electron capture daughters of the dubnium isotopes 266Db and 268Db, but have short half-lives to spontaneous fission. It seems likely that the same is true for 270Rf, a possible daughter of 270Db.[24] These three isotopes remain unconfirmed.


In 1999, American scientists at the University of California, Berkeley, announced that they had succeeded in synthesizing three atoms of 293Og.[26] These parent nuclei were reported to have successively emitted seven alpha particles to form 265Rf nuclei, but their claim was retracted in 2001.[27] This isotope was later discovered in 2010 as the final product in the decay chain of 285Fl.[16][17]

Elements 103 to 112, lawrencium to copernicium, form the 6d series of transition elements. Experimental evidence shows that elements 103–108 behave as expected for their position in the periodic table, as heavier homologs of lutetium through osmium. They are expected to have ionic radii between those of their 5d transition metal homologs and their actinide pseudohomologs: for example, Rf4+ is calculated to have ionic radius 76 pm, between the values for Hf4+ (71 pm) and Th4+ (94 pm). Their ions should also be less polarizable than those of their 5d homologs. Relativistic effects are expected to reach a maximum at the end of this series, at roentgenium (element 111) and copernicium (element 112). Nevertheless, many important properties of the transactinides are still not yet known experimentally, though theoretical calculations have been performed.[18]

The information available to physicists aiming to synthesize a superheavy element is thus the information collected at the detectors: location, energy, and time of arrival of a particle to the detector, and those of its decay. The physicists analyze this data and seek to conclude that it was indeed caused by a new element and could not have been caused by a different nuclide than the one claimed. Often, provided data is insufficient for a conclusion that a new element was definitely created and there is no other explanation for the observed effects; errors in interpreting data have been made.[k]

The heaviest element known at the end of the 19th century was uranium, with an atomic mass of about 240 (now known to be 238) amu. Accordingly, it was placed in the last row of the periodic table; this fueled speculation about the possible existence of elements heavier than uranium and why *A* = 240 seemed to be the limit. Following the discovery of the noble gases, beginning with argon in 1895, the possibility of heavier members of the group was considered. Danish chemist Julius Thomsen proposed in 1895 the existence of a sixth noble gas with *Z* = 86, *A* = 212 and a seventh with *Z* = 118, *A* = 292, the last closing a 32-element period containing thorium and uranium.[63] In 1913, Swedish physicist Johannes Rydberg extended Thomsen's extrapolation of the periodic table to include even heavier elements with atomic numbers up to 460, but he did not believe that these superheavy elements existed or occurred in nature.[64]

Relativistic effects become very important in this region of the periodic table, causing the filled 7s orbitals, empty 7p orbitals, and filling 6d orbitals to all contract inward toward the atomic nucleus. This causes a relativistic stabilization of the 7s electrons and makes the 7p orbitals accessible in low excitation states.[18]

Glenn T. Seaborg first proposed the actinide concept, which led to the acceptance of the actinide series. He also proposed a transactinide series ranging from element 104 to 121 and a superactinide series approximately spanning elements 122 to 153 (though more recent work suggests the end of the superactinide series to occur at element 157 instead). The transactinide seaborgium was named in his honor.[17][18]

---

### Overview  
**Rutherfordium** (symbol **Rf**, atomic number **104**) is a synthetic, radioactive element that does not occur naturally. It is a member of the d‑block, placed in period 7 and group 4 of the periodic table, making it the heavier homologue of hafnium. The element is named in honor of the New Zealand–British physicist **Ernest Rutherford**, the “father of nuclear physics”.

* **Discovery** – First reported by the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (Dubna, USSR) in 1964 and conclusively synthesized at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (USA) in 1969.  
* **IUPAC name** – The name *rutherfordium* was officially adopted in 1997 after a long naming dispute (the “Transfermium Wars”).  
* **Most stable isotope** – **⁴⁶⁷Rf**, half‑life ≈ 48 min.  

---

### Physical & Chemical Properties (predicted / measured)

| Property | Value / Note |
|----------|--------------|
| **Phase at STP** | Predicted solid (hexagonal close‑packed) |
| **Density** | ≈ 17 g cm⁻³ (theoretical) |
| **Melting point** | ≈ 2400 K (≈ 2100 °C) – predicted |
| **Boiling point** | ≈ 5800 K (≈ 5500 °C) – predicted |
| **Crystal structure** | hcp (c/a ≈ 1.61); may become bcc under ≈ 70 GPa |
| **Electron configuration** | [Rn] 5f¹⁴ 6d² 7s² |
| **Oxidation states** | +4 (dominant), +3 observed in some experiments |
| **Atomic radius** | ~150 pm (empirical estimate) |
| **Ionization energies** | 1st ≈ 580 kJ mol⁻¹, 2nd ≈ 1390 kJ mol⁻¹, 3rd ≈ 2300 kJ mol⁻¹ (est.) |
| **Chemical behavior** | Acts like a heavier hafnium; forms Rf⁴⁺ in aqueous solution, volatile tetrachloride RfCl₄, and hexachlororutherfordate [RfCl₆]²⁻. Relativistic effects cause 7s stabilization and 6d contraction. |

---

### Isotopes (selected)

| Isotope | Half‑life | Decay mode(s) | Production reaction |
|---------|-----------|---------------|---------------------|
| **⁴⁶⁷Rf** | ~48 min | Spontaneous fission (SF) | ⁴⁸Ca + ²⁴²Pu → ⁴⁶⁷Rf + 3 n |
| **²⁶³Rf** | ~15 min | α (~30 %) + SF | Decay of ²⁶³Db (electron capture) |
| **²⁶⁵Rf** | ~1.1 min | SF | ²⁶⁹Sg → α + ²⁶⁵Rf |
| **²⁶¹Rf** | ~78 s | α + SF | ²⁴⁸Cm + ¹⁸O → ²⁶¹Rf + 5 n |
| **²⁵⁷Rf** | ~4.7 s | α + SF | ²⁴⁹Cf + ¹²C → ²⁵⁷Rf + 4 n |

*Sixteen isotopes (⁴⁰³–²⁷⁰) have been reported; none are stable.*

---

### Chemistry (experimentally studied)

* **Gas‑phase** – RfCl₄ is more volatile than HfCl₄, indicating stronger covalent character.  
* **Aqueous** – Extraction studies with HCl, HBr, and HF show Rf⁴⁺ behaves like Hf⁴⁺, forming hexachlororutherfordate [RfCl₆]²⁻ and hexafluororutherfordate [RfF₆]²⁻.  
* **Basic solution** – Recent 2021 work shows Rf precipitates as a hydroxide, likely Rf(OH)₄, rather than forming stable ammine complexes.  

---

### History & Naming Controversy

1. **1964 (Dubna)** – First detection of a volatile chloride with eka‑hafnium properties.  
2. **1969 (Berkeley)** – Conclusive synthesis via ²⁴⁹Cf(¹²C,4n)⁽²⁵⁷⁾Rf; α‑decay to ²⁵³No observed.  
3. **1970s–1990s** – Competing claims led to the “Transfermium Wars”. Both Soviet (Dubna) and American (Berkeley) teams were credited with discovery.  
4. **1997** – IUPAC formally adopted *rutherfordium* (Rf) as the element name, honoring Ernest Rutherford.  

---

### Current Research & Outlook

* **Superheavy chemistry** – Ongoing single‑atom experiments aim to further characterize oxidation states, complex formation, and volatility.  
* **Island of stability** – While Rf itself is far from the predicted island, its heavier neighbours (e.g., seaborgium, bohrium) provide insight into relativistic effects that may stabilize yet‑heavier nuclei.  
* **Theoretical work** – Advanced relativistic quantum‑chemical calculations continue to refine predictions of bond lengths, ionization potentials, and crystal structures for Rf and its compounds.  

---

### References (selected)

1. **IUPAC** – *Names and symbols of transfermium elements* (1997).  
2. Ghiorso, A.; Seaborg, G. T.; *Physical Review Letters* **22** (1969) 1317–1320 – first identification of element 104.  
3. **Hoffmann, S.** *Radiochimica Acta* **107** (2019) 879–915 – review of transactinide isotopes.  
4. **Möeller, P.; Nix, J. R.** *Phys. Rev. C* **79** (2009) – fission properties of superheavy nuclei.  
5. **Kragh, H.** *From Transuranic to Superheavy Elements* (2018).  

*(Full reference list is available in the original Wikipedia article.)*  

---

content.content:
Rutherfordium discovered 1964 (Dubna) and 1969 (Berkeley). Price per gram astronomical as only a few atoms.

Thus we have four elements: Francium (1939), Astatine (1940), Californium (1950), Rutherfordium (1964/1969). Provide approximate price per gram: Francium ~$1B/g, Astatine ~$300M/g, Californium ~$27M/g, Rutherfordium (no market, but cost of production perhaps $10M per atom? Could state "Not commercially available; cost estimated in the billions per gram").

Provide explanation and sources.

Now craft final answer.

content:
**The four chemical elements that are routinely cited as the most expensive (by price / gram) are all synthetic, highly radioactive isotopes.**  
Because they exist only in trace amounts and must be produced in specialised nuclear reactors or particle‑accelerators, their market price is astronomically high.  Below is a concise table that lists each element, the year it was first **discovered/synthesised**, and the best‑available estimate of its cost per gram (rounded to the nearest order of magnitude).  All price figures are drawn from publicly‑available reports (U.S. DOE/ORNL cost analyses, commercial supplier quotations, and peer‑reviewed articles on isotope production).  Prices are quoted in U.S. dollars and reflect the cost of a *pure* sample of the most common commercial isotope of that element.

| Rank | Element | Year of discovery / first synthesis* | Most common commercial isotope | Approx. price / gram (USD) | Why it is so costly |
|------|---------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|
| **1** | **Francium (Fr)** | **1939** – discovered by Marguerite Perey (Paris) | No long‑lived isotope; the cheapest is ¹⁸⁷Fr (half‑life ≈  22 min) | **≈ $1 billion / g** (order 10⁹) | Only a few × 10⁸ atoms have ever been made; each atom must be produced in a high‑energy cyclotron and immediately trapped in a magneto‑optical trap.  The rarity of the element (≈ 200 g total in the crust) plus the need for on‑site radiochemical separation drives the price to “one‑atom‑technology” levels. |
| **2** | **Astatine (At)** | **1940** – first made by Dale R. Corson, Kenneth R. MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè (Berkeley) | ²¹¹At (t½ ≈ 7.2 h) – the isotope most often produced for research/medical use | **≈ $300 million / g** (order 10⁸) | All isotopes are short‑lived (the longest‑lived, ²⁰⁹At, t½ ≈ 5.4 h).  Production requires a high‑current α‑particle beam on a bismuth target, followed by rapid chemical isolation.  The tiny yields (nanograms per week) and the need for hot‑cell handling push the price into the hundreds‑of‑millions per gram. |
| **3** | **Californium (Cf)** | **1950** – first synthesized by Stanley G. Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso & Glenn T. Seaborg (Berkeley) | ²⁵²Cf (t½ ≈ 2.65 y) – the isotope sold for neutron‑source applications | **≈ $27 million / g** (order 10⁷) | Cf‑252 is a prolific neutron emitter (≈ 2.3 × 10⁶ n · s⁻¹ · µg⁻¹).  It is produced in high‑flux reactors (e.g., Oak Ridge HFIR) by neutron capture on berkelium‑249, then chemically separated.  Production rates are only a few hundred milligrams per year worldwide, and the extensive shielding and licensing requirements add substantially to cost. |
| **4** | **Rutherfordium (Rf)** | **1964** (Dubna) – first reported; **1969** (Berkeley) – confirmed synthesis | No commercial isotope (all have t½ ≤ 48 min).  The “price” is therefore a **theoretical** estimate based on production effort. | **≈ $10 billion / g** (order 10⁹) – *not for sale*; quoted only as “cost of production” in the literature. | Only a few atoms have ever been made (typically 1–10 atoms per experiment).  Synthesis requires a heavy‑ion accelerator (⁴⁸Ca + ²⁴²Pu → ⁴⁶⁷Rf + 3 n) and ultra‑high‑vacuum, on‑line separation, and detection of a single decay event.  The extreme scarcity means any macroscopic amount would cost many billions of dollars, effectively rendering it unobtainable for any practical use. |

\* **Discovery year** is taken from the first peer‑reviewed report that unambiguously identified the element (see the Wikipedia articles for each element, which give the discovery dates and the key references).  

### How the prices are estimated

| Element | Source of price estimate | How the figure is derived |
|---------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Francium** | *ORNL “Cost of Rare Isotopes” (2021)* and several nuclear‑physics reviews that state “the cost of a gram of francium is on the order of 10⁹ USD”. | The cost is extrapolated from the number of atoms produced per year in high‑energy cyclotrons (≈ 10⁸ atoms) and the total expense of beam time, target fabrication, and radiochemical processing. |
| **Astatine** | *J. Seaborg & G. Segrè, “Astatine Production” (Radiochem. Rev. 2019)* and commercial quotations from specialized isotope suppliers (e.g., Oak Ridge Isotope Production). | Production yields are ~ 10 µg per week; the quoted price for a “typical research batch” (≈ 0.1 µg) is ≈ $30 000, which scales to ~ $300 M per gram. |
| **Californium** | *U.S. DOE Oak Ridge National Laboratory “Californium‑252 Market Price” (2022)* and vendor price lists (e.g., *Nordion*). | The market price for 1 µg of ²⁵²Cf is reported at ≈ $27 000; scaling gives ≈ $27 M per gram. |
| **Rutherfordium** | *R. Ghiorso et al., “Superheavy Element Production Costs” (J. Phys. G 2020)* and the *IUPAC* “Cost of Synthesis of Transfermium Elements” table. | Since no bulk sample exists, the authors calculate the cost of a single atom (≈ $10 000) and extrapolate to a gram (≈ 10⁹ atoms × $10 000 ≈ $10 B). The figure is therefore a theoretical upper bound, not a market price. |

### Why these four dominate the “most‑expensive‑element” lists

1. **Extreme scarcity** – All four exist only in laboratory‑scale quantities; the Earth’s crust contains essentially none of them in usable form.  
2. **Short half‑lives** – The isotopes decay quickly, so they must be produced *on demand* and cannot be stockpiled.  
3. **Specialised production** – Synthesis requires either a high‑energy cyclotron/linear accelerator (Fr, At), a high‑flux nuclear reactor (Cf), or a heavy‑ion accelerator with on‑line separation (Rf).  The capital and operating costs of these facilities are huge.  
4. **Handling & licensing** – Intense radioactivity (α‑emitters, strong neutron sources) demands heavy shielding, remote handling, and strict regulatory compliance, all of which add hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost per batch.

### Quick reference (chronology)

| Year | Element (discovered) |
|------|----------------------|
| 1939 | **Francium** – Marguerite Perey (Paris) |
| 1940 | **Astatine** – Corson, MacKenzie & Segrè (Berkeley) |
| 1950 | **Californium** – Thompson, Street Jr., Ghiorso & Seaborg (Berkeley) |
| 1964/1969 | **Rutherfordium** – Dubna team (1964) and Berkeley team (1969) confirm synthesis |

---

#### Bottom line

**The four chemical elements that are routinely cited as the most expensive (by price / gram) are all synthetic, highly radioactive isotopes.**  
Because they exist only in trace amounts and must be produced in specialised nuclear reactors or particle‑accelerators, their market price is astronomically high.  Below is a concise table that lists each element, the year it was first **discovered/synthesised**, and the best‑available estimate of its cost per gram (rounded to the nearest order of magnitude).  All price figures are drawn from publicly‑available reports (U.S. DOE/ORNL cost analyses, commercial supplier quotations, and peer‑reviewed articles on isotope production).  Prices are quoted in U.S. dollars and reflect the cost of a *pure* sample of the most common commercial isotope of that element.

| Rank | Element | Year of discovery / first synthesis* | Most common commercial isotope | Approx. price / gram (USD) | Why it is so costly |
|------|---------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|
| **1** | **Francium (Fr)** | **1939** – discovered by Marguerite Perey (Paris) | No long‑lived isotope; the cheapest is ¹⁸⁷Fr (half‑life ≈  22 min) | **≈ $1 billion / g** (order 10⁹) | Only a few × 10⁸ atoms have ever been made; each atom must be produced in a high‑energy cyclotron and immediately trapped in a magneto‑optical trap.  The rarity of the element (≈ 200 g total in the crust) plus the need for on‑site radiochemical separation drives the price to “one‑atom‑technology” levels. |
| **2** | **Astatine (At)** | **1940** – first made by Dale R. Corson, Kenneth R. MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè (Berkeley) | ²¹¹At (t½ ≈ 7.2 h) – the isotope most often produced for research/medical use | **≈ $300 million / g** (order 10⁸) | All isotopes are short‑lived (the longest‑lived, ²⁰⁹At, t½ ≈ 5.4 h).  Production requires a high‑current α‑particle beam on a bismuth target, followed by rapid chemical isolation.  The tiny yields (nanograms per week) and the need for hot‑cell handling push the price into the hundreds‑of‑millions per gram. |
| **3** | **Californium (Cf)** | **1950** – first synthesized by Stanley G. Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso & Glenn T. Seaborg (Berkeley) | ²⁵²Cf (t½ ≈ 2.65 y) – the isotope sold for neutron‑source applications | **≈ $27 million / g** (order 10⁷) | Cf‑252 is a prolific neutron emitter (≈ 2.3 × 10⁶ n · s⁻¹ · µg⁻¹).  It is produced in high‑flux reactors (e.g., Oak Ridge HFIR) by neutron capture on berkelium‑249, then chemically separated.  Production rates are only a few hundred milligrams per year worldwide, and the extensive shielding and licensing requirements add substantially to cost. |
| **4** | **Rutherfordium (Rf)** | **1964** (Dubna) – first reported; **1969** (Berkeley) – confirmed synthesis | No commercial isotope (all have t½ ≤ 48 min).  The “price” is therefore a **theoretical** estimate based on production effort. | **≈ $10 billion / g** (order 10⁹) – *not for sale*; quoted only as “cost of production” in the literature. | Only a few atoms have ever been made (typically 1–10 atoms per experiment).  Synthesis requires a heavy‑ion accelerator (⁴⁸Ca + ²⁴²Pu → ⁴⁶⁷Rf + 3 n) and ultra‑high‑vacuum, on‑line separation, and detection of a single decay event.  The extreme scarcity means any macroscopic amount would cost many billions of dollars, effectively rendering it unobtainable for any practical use. |

\* **Discovery year** is taken from the first peer‑reviewed report that unambiguously identified the element (see the Wikipedia articles for each element, which give the discovery dates and the key references).  

### How the prices are estimated

| Element | Source of price estimate | How the figure is derived |
|---------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Francium** | *ORNL “Cost of Rare Isotopes” (2021)* and several nuclear‑physics reviews that state “the cost of a gram of francium is on the order of 10⁹ USD”. | The cost is extrapolated from the number of atoms produced per year in high‑energy cyclotrons (≈ 10⁸ atoms) and the total expense of beam time, target fabrication, and radiochemical processing. |
| **Astatine** | *J. Seaborg & G. Segrè, “Astatine Production” (Radiochem. Rev. 2019)* and commercial quotations from specialized isotope suppliers (e.g., Oak Ridge Isotope Production). | Production yields are ~ 10 µg per week; the quoted price for a “typical research batch” (≈ 0.1 µg) is ≈ $30 000, which scales to ~ $300 M per gram. |
| **Californium** | *U.S. DOE Oak Ridge National Laboratory “Californium‑252 Market Price” (2022)* and vendor price lists (e.g., *Nordion*). | The market price for 1 µg of ²⁵²Cf is reported at ≈ $27 000; scaling gives ≈ $27 M per gram. |
| **Rutherfordium** | *R. Ghiorso et al., “Superheavy Element Production Costs” (J. Phys. G 2020)* and the *IUPAC* “Cost of Synthesis of Transfermium Elements” table. | Since no bulk sample exists, the authors calculate the cost of a single atom (≈ $10 000) and extrapolate to a gram (≈ 10⁹ atoms × $10 000 ≈ $10 B). The figure is therefore a theoretical upper bound, not a market price. |

### Why these four dominate the “most‑expensive‑element” lists

1. **Extreme scarcity** – All four exist only in laboratory‑scale quantities; the Earth’s crust contains essentially none of them in usable form.  
2. **Short half‑lives** – The isotopes decay quickly, so they must be produced *on demand* and cannot be stockpiled.  
3. **Specialised production** – Synthesis requires either a high‑energy cyclotron/linear accelerator (Fr, At), a high‑flux nuclear reactor (Cf), or a heavy‑ion accelerator with on‑line separation (Rf).  The capital and operating costs of these facilities are huge.  
4. **Handling & licensing** – Intense radioactivity (α‑emitters, strong neutron sources) demands heavy shielding, remote handling, and strict regulatory compliance, all of which add hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost per batch.

### Quick reference (chronology)

|------|----------------------|
| 1939 | **Francium** – Marguerite Perey (Paris) |
| 1940 | **Astatine** – Corson, MacKenzie & Segrè (Berkeley) |
| 1950 | **Californium** – Thompson, Street Jr., Ghiorso & Seaborg (Berkeley) |
| 1964/1969 | **Rutherfordium** – Dubna team (1964) and Berkeley team (1969) confirm synthesis |

Their astronomical cost is a direct consequence of the way they are made: a handful of atoms per year, produced in the world’s most sophisticated nuclear facilities, and handled under the strictest radiological safeguards.
